A blotch is a large, messy, irregularly shaped mark or patch that appears on a surface or on skin. Think of it as a mark that looks accidental, clumsy, or out of place — something that stands out because it doesn't belong or because it looks like something went wrong.
The defining features of a blotch

Irregular shape. This is the most important quality. A blotch has no clean, neat edges. It isn't round, square, or any recognizable shape — its edges are ragged, uneven, and random-looking, like a mark made carelessly or by accident.

Noticeable contrast. A blotch stands out visually because it's a different color from the surface around it. It catches your eye precisely because it doesn't match its surroundings.

A reasonable size. A blotch is bigger than a tiny dot or speck. It covers a meaningful area — it has some spread to it.

An unwanted, messy quality. This is the heart of the word. A blotch always carries a sense of something unplanned, unsightly, or unfortunate. You wouldn't use this word to describe something that looks intentional or neat.

On paper or fabric. If a fountain pen leaks onto a notebook, the result is a blotch of ink — an irregular, spreading stain with no clean shape. A spill of paint on a shirt creates a blotch.

On skin. This is one of the most common uses. After a rash, sunburn, allergic reaction, or from heat or cold, you might develop blotches on your skin — irregular, discolored patches, often reddish or purplish, scattered unevenly across an area. A person who blushes easily might get blotches of red on their face and neck rather than an even flush of color.

On walls, floors, or surfaces. A water leak on a ceiling leaves a blotch. An uneven patch of paint on a wall is a blotch.

On animals and plants. Some animals have blotches in their coat — irregular patches of a contrasting color, larger and less defined than a proper "spot." Diseased leaves in plants often develop blotches — irregular areas of yellow, brown, or black discoloration.
How it differs from similar words

Blotch vs. spot. A spot is smaller and more defined — often roughly round, with cleaner edges, and it can even look intentional (like a polka dot). A blotch is larger and sloppier. Dalmatian dogs have spots; a stain left by a spilled drink is a blotch.

Blotch vs. stain. A stain emphasizes the cause — something soaked into a material and discolored it (a coffee stain, a rust stain). A blotch emphasizes the appearance — how it looks: big, irregular, and messy. A stain can look like a blotch, but the word "blotch" says nothing about what caused it. A birthmark on someone's skin is a blotch, not a stain.

Blotch vs. patch. A patch is neutral — it simply means an area that differs from its surroundings, without any negative meaning. A patch of sunlight, a patch of green grass. A blotch, by contrast, always implies that something looks bad or wrong. Every blotch could loosely be called a patch, but not every patch is a blotch.

Blotch vs. smear. A smear is elongated and directional — it looks like something was dragged or wiped across a surface. A blotch is more settled and spread out, without that sense of direction.
The tone and connotation of the word

"Blotch" is an inherently negative, unattractive word. It's never used to describe something beautiful or purposeful. Calling something a blotch implies it looks bad — clumsy, unfortunate, or out of place. The word itself sounds a little harsh and ugly, which matches what it describes.

• There was a dark blotch of ink on the letter where his pen had leaked.
  • She noticed red blotches spreading across her neck from the allergic reaction.
  • The old photograph had a large blotch of water damage in the corner.
  • The puppy was mostly white, with a single brown blotch across its left ear.
  • The damp patch on the ceiling had grown into an ugly blotch overnight.
  • His face was flushed and blotchy after the long run — uneven patches of red everywhere.

If you want one image to anchor this word: imagine someone accidentally knocking over a jar of ink. The liquid spreads outward in an uneven, irregular puddle — no clean shape, no clean edges, just an unwanted, conspicuous mess on the page. That is a blotch. The word captures exactly that quality — something large, irregular, visually disruptive, and almost always unwanted — whether it's on paper, skin, fabric, or any other surface.
